title: 2  Meet Your Instructor

2.1 About
Chair, Department of Economics | rmcnab@odu.edu | 757-683-3153
Professor Robert M. McNab currently serves as the Chair of the Department of Economics in the Strome College of Business at Old Dominion University. Dr. McNab is also the Director of the Dragas Center for Economic Analysis and Policy at Old Dominion University. He is a member of the Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia’s Survey of Professional Forecasters and, from 2018 to 2022, he was a member of the Joint Advisory Board of Economists for the Commonwealth of Virginia. Professor McNab has published in Applied Economics, Cornell Hospitality Quarterly, Defense and Peace Economics, National Tax Journal, Public Budgeting and Finance, and World Development, among others. He edits the annual State of the Region: Hampton Roads and State of the Commonwealth reports Professor McNab has appeared in the Associated Press, China Global Television Network, CNN, LiveNow from Fox News, Forbes, Newsweek, Wall Street Journal, Washington Post, Welt am Sonntag, Yahoo News, Yahoo Finance, Richmond Times-Dispatch, Virginian Pilot, Virginia Public Media, and Daily Press, among others. Dr. McNab joined the faculty of the Department of Economics in the Strome College of Business of Old Dominion University in July 2016 and previously was a member of the faculty of the Naval Postgraduate School in Monterey, California from 2000 to 2016.

title: 2  Meet Your Instructor

2.2 Contact Policy
Students should feel welcome to contact me via email at rmcnab@odu.edu or drop by Zoom office hours. I strongly encourage students to communicate with me. I will try to answer emails within 48 business hours (often much sooner) for course related topics.
Students should take the time to craft complete, professional emails. The more information that you can provide about a question or problem, the more likely that my response will be helpful. Avoid non-professional language and practice communicating in the corporate workplace. Emails that are unprofessional will be returned with no action.
Students should proactively address issues with the class and scheduling rather than waiting until an assignment or case study discussion is overdue. In many cases, accommodations can be made for ‘life events,’ however, clear and prompt communication is necessary.

title: 3  Course Objectives
text: 3.1 Course Learning Objectives (CLOs)

title: 3  Course Objectives
text:
CLO 1: Derive the Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) estimators to establish a foundation of econometric techniques.
CLO 2: Identify critical econometric issues, including omitted variable bias, heteroscedasticity, multicollinearity, and endogeneity, to determine the validity of the linear regression model.
CLO 3: Conduct hypothesis testing (including t-tests, F-tests, and Wald tests) and interpret regression estimates to investigate economic and social phenomena.
CLO 4: Evaluate the small sample and asymptotic properties of estimators, specifically focusing on the concepts of unbiasedness, consistency, and efficiency.
CLO 5: Utilize R and RStudio to implement statistical techniques and effectively communicate results through reproducible code, visualizations, and written analysis.

title: 3  Course Objectives
text:
3.2 Textbooks and Materials
The required textbook is an integral part of the class. Students should expect to read the textbook prior to each module and to be prepared to answer discussion questions from the textbook. The textbook provides the foundation upon which the course is built and students will succeed if they take the time to read and review the material in the textbook.
As this course focuses on the learning and application of statistical techniques, a computer with R and R Studio installed is necessary. You will need access to a laptop, tablet, or other computing device to complete the assignments and exams.
You may also use R Studio Cloud instead of a locally installed version of R.
You can create a free R-Studio cloud if you do not want to use a locally installed version of R and R Studio.
All other course materials are on Canvas or can be accessed through Canvas. You are required to know how to use Canvas to access and submit assignments, quizzes, and examinations. You should also be comfortable using ODU email to communicate.

title: 4  Module 1 Overview
text:
4.1 Introduction
Welcome to Module 1 of ECON 706.
In this module, we will briefly review matrix operations before introducing the multiple variable linear regression model. We will discuss the assumptions of the multiple variable linear regression model, the assumptions of the model, and consequences associated with the violations of these assumptions. We will then use R to estimate a naive multiple variable linear regression model.

title: 4  Module 1 Overview
text:
4.2 Learning Objectives
By the end of this module, you should be able to:

MLO 1: Apply descriptive statistics for initial data exploration.
MLO 2: Define the notation and concepts used to construct the linear regression model.
MLO 3: Identify the core assumptions of the classical linear regression model.
MLO 4: Discuss the consequences of the violations of the core assumptions of the model.
MLO 5: Apply R and R Studio to obtain, clean, and estimate a naive linear regression model.

title: 5  Matrix Operations
text:
5.1 Matrix Operations
This module covers the essential matrix operations required for econometrics. We begin with basic matrix creation and arithmetic, progressing to more complex operations like inversion and formal multiplication. Understanding these operations is critical as they form the backbone of the Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) estimator, which we will derive and implement both manually and using built-in R functions.

title: 5  Matrix Operations
text:
5.2 Matrix Creation
We can create two vectors that contain 4 numeric elements and form two matrices that are \((2 \times 2)\) Assume that we have call the two matrices, \(m_1\) and \(m_2\) and the matrices can be expressed as:
\[ m_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 6 \\ 4 & 8 \end{bmatrix} \]
\[ m_2 = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & 2 \\ 15 & 12 \end{bmatrix} \]
We can also create a \((4 \times 1)\) matrix from the same elements that form \(m_1\) or:
\[
m_{1a} = \begin{bmatrix}
2 \\
4 \\
6 \\
8
\end{bmatrix}
\]
We can take a transpose of a matrix by using t(), so t(m_1) would be the transpose of matrix m_1 or
\[
m_1^T = \begin{bmatrix}
2 & 4 \\
6 & 8
\end{bmatrix}
\]
We can use the dim function to obtain the dimensions of a matrix (and other elements like vectors).

title: 5  Matrix Operations
text:
5.3 Matrix Addition
In this example, we demonstrate how to add matrices.
We return to the two \((2 \times 2)\) matrices in the previous example and add the matrices together.
\[ \begin{bmatrix}
2 & 6 \\ 4 & 8
\end{bmatrix} +
\begin{bmatrix}
5 & 2 \\ 15 & 12
\end{bmatrix} =
\begin{bmatrix}
(2 + 5) & (6 + 2) \\
(4 + 15) & (8 + 12)
\end{bmatrix} =
\begin{bmatrix}
7 & 8 \\
19 & 20
\end{bmatrix}\]
When we add \(m_1\) and \(m_2\), we are adding the values in the same position in each matrix.
For example, for \(m_1\), the value in the first row, first column is equal to 2.
For \(m_2\), the value in the first row, first column is equal to 5.
Adding \(m_1\) and \(m_2\) yields a value of 7 in the first row, first column of the resulting matrix.
The order for matrix addition does not matter, that is, \(m_1 + m_2 = m_2 + m_1\).

title: 5  Matrix Operations
text:
5.4 Matrix Subtraction
Using a similar process, we can subtract one matrix from another. While order does not matter for addition, order does matter for subtraction.
If we subtract \(m_2\) from \(m_1\), that is \(m_1 - m_2\), then, we are subtracting the value of each element in \(m_2\) from the corresponding element in \(m_1\).
\[ \begin{bmatrix}
2 & 6 \\ 4 & 8
\end{bmatrix} -
\begin{bmatrix}
5 & 2 \\ 15 & 12
\end{bmatrix} =
\begin{bmatrix}
(2 - 5) & (6 - 2) \\
(4 - 15) & (8 - 12)
\end{bmatrix} =
\begin{bmatrix}
-3 & 4 \\
-11 & -4
\end{bmatrix}\]
The value in the first row, first column of \(m_1\) is equal to 5. When we subtract \(m_2\) from \(m_1\), we would subtract 2 (first row, first column of \(m_2\)) from 5 (first row, first column of \(m_1\)), that is, the resulting value is equal to \(2-5 = -3\).
On the other hand, if we subtract \(m_1\) from \(m_2\), then the same position yields \(5-2 = 3\).
\[ \begin{bmatrix}
5 & 2 \\ 15 & 12
\end{bmatrix} -
\begin{bmatrix}
2 & 6 \\ 4 & 8
\end{bmatrix} -
=
\begin{bmatrix}
(5 - 2) & (2 - 6) \\
(15 - 4) & (12 - 8)
\end{bmatrix} =
\begin{bmatrix}
3 & -4 \\
11 & 4
\end{bmatrix}\]

title: 5  Matrix Operations
text:
5.5 Hadamard Product
Element-by-element matrix multiplication is straightforward but is not typically used in this class. Element-by-element matrix multiplication is known as the Hadamard Product.
The order of multiplication does not matter, however, the two matrices must have identical dimensions.
Returning to the two matrices, \(m_1\) and \(m_2\), we can conduct element-by-element multiplication by multiplying each element by its corresponding element in the other matrix.
\[
m1 \times m2 =
\begin{bmatrix}
2 & 6 \\
4 & 8
\end{bmatrix} \times
\begin{bmatrix}
5 & 2 \\
15 & 12
\end{bmatrix} =
\begin{bmatrix}
(2 \times 5) & (6 \times 2) \\
(4 \times 15) & (8 \times 12)
\end{bmatrix} =
\begin{bmatrix}
10 & 12 \\
60 & 96
\end{bmatrix}
\]
As an exercise, you can use the webr code chunk below to calculate the product of the two matrices and observe whether the Hadamard Product depends on the order of multiplication.

title: 5  Matrix Operations
text:
5.6 Matrix Multiplication
If A is a \((m \times n)\) matrix and B is a \((n \times p)\) matrix, then we can form the matrix product C by AB, if and only if the two matrices are compatible.
The first step is to ensure the matrices are compatible, that is, the inner dimensions of the matrices must match. In this case, the columns in A are equal to the rows in B, so the matrices are compatible.
The resulting matrix will have the dimensions of the ‘outer’ numbers. If we examine this from a dimensional perspective then:
\[
A \times B = (m \times n) \times (n \times p) = (m \times p)
\]
For example, assume that A is \((5 \times 5)\) and B is \((5 \times 8)\). We can form the matrix product AB since the as the number of columns in A is equal to the number of rows in B.

We cannot, however, form the matrix product BA since the number of columns in B is not equal to the number of rows in A.
In general, the only time we are assured that we can multiply AB and BA is when A and B are square matrices with the same dimensions.
Recall that we have previously defined two matrices as:
\[
m_1 = \begin{bmatrix}
2 & 6 \\
4 & 8
\end{bmatrix}\]
\[m_2 = \begin{bmatrix}
5 & 2 \\
15 & 12
\end{bmatrix}
\]
Step 1: Top-Left element: Take the first row of \(m_1\) and multiply it by the first column of \(m_2\).
\[
(2 \times 5) + (6 \times 15) = 10 + 90 = 100
\]
Step 2: Top-Right Element: Take the first row of \(m_1\) and multiply it by the second column of \(m_2\).
\[
(2 \times 2) + (6 \times 12) = 4 + 72 = 76
\]
Step 3: Bottom-Left element: Take the second row of \(m_1\) and multiply it by the first column of \(m_2\).
\[
(4 \times 5) + (8 \times 15) = 20 + 120 = 140
\]
Step 4: Bottom-right element: Take the second row of \(m_1\) and multiply it by the second column of \(m_2\).
\[
(4 \times 2) + (8 \times 12) = 8 + 96 = 104
\]
When we multiply \(m_1\) by \(m_2\) we obtain a new matrix that is the matrix product or
\[
m_1m_2 = \begin{bmatrix}
2 & 6 \\
4 & 8
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}
5 & 2 \\
15 & 12
\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
(2 \times 5) + (6 \times 15) & (2 \times 2) + (6 \times 12) \\
(4 \times 5) + (8 \times 15) & (4 \times 2) + (8 \times 12)
\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
100 & 76 \\
140 & 104
\end{bmatrix}
\]
To illustrate the point that, in general, matrix multiplication depends on the order of the matrices, we can calculate the product of \(m_2 m_1\).
Step 1: Top-Left element: Take the first row of \(m_2\) and multiply it by the first column of \(m_1\).
\[ (5 \times 2) + (2 \times 4) = 10 + 8 = 18 \]
Step 2: Top-Right Element: Take the first row of \(m_2\) and multiply it by the second column of \(m_1\).
\[ (5 \times 6) + (2 \times 8) = 30 + 16 = 46 \]
Step 3: Bottom-Left element: Take the second row of \(m_2\) and multiply it by the first column of \(m_1\).
\[ (15 \times 2) + (12 \times 4) = 30 + 48 = 78 \]
Step 4: Bottom-right element: Take the second row of \(m_1\) and multiply it by the second column of \(m_2\).
\[ (15 \times 6) + (12 \times 8) = 186 \]
When we multiply \(m_1\) by \(m_2\) we obtain a new matrix that is the matrix product or
\[ m_2 m_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & 2 \\ 15 & 12  \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 6 \\ 4 & 8  \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} (5 \times 2) + (2 \times 4) & (5 \times 6) + (2 \times 8) \\ (15 \times 2) + (12 \times 4) & (15 \times 6) + (12 \times 8) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 18 & 46 \\ 78 & 186 \end{bmatrix} \]
This illustrates the point: matrix multiplication is non-communicative. Comparability and order of operations matter. Change the order, obtain a different result.
